newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli markets rattled by Netanyahu scandal.
newsitem.headline: Israeli markets rattled by Netanyahu scandal.

text.p: Israeli shares, bonds and the shekel currency fell on Thursday in response to news that police had recommended charging Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with fraud and breach of trust.
The Tel Aviv stock market's main index fell by nearly two percent and investors fled the local currency for the relative safety of the dollar.
"People are selling shekels and buying dollars, there is a fear that maybe foreign investors will flee," said a dealer at Israel Discount Bank.
Analysts said the markets would remain bumpy, and foreign investors sidelined, until the clouds cleared after Wednesday's announcement, which newspapers tagged a "political bombshell".

It is up to Israel's state prosecutor to decide whether or not to implement the police recommendation over Netanyahu's short-lived appointment of an attorney general in January. A swift decision has been promised.
In the early morning, the shekel fell to as low as 3.421 shekels to the dollar before recovering slightly to 3.404, against Wednesday's representative rate of 3.398.

The stock market opened with almost 80 million shekels in supply versus only three million in demand, indicating aggressive selling by investors. The benchmark Mishtanim index of top 100 shares closed down 1.97 percent, or 5.02 points, at 249.27.
The news also took its toll on the Israeli bond market, with government paper closing lower.
"There is uncertainty in the market. The political situation is such that economic issues will not be at the centre of the government's attention," said a trader at a big financial company.
The scandal first emerged in January and although it cast a shadow over the Israeli stock market, until now it weathered the growing storm relatively unscathed.

"The market was extremely resilient until yesterday. If it blows over, the market will resume momentum but if there are new elections that period will be very uncertain," said Daniella Finn of Batucha Securities.
Stephen Levey of London-based Carnegie Emerging Markets said the next few days would present a good buying opportunity if there is a serious correction in the market.
"We may see foreign activity declining over a certain period, but in the cold light of day it doesn't look too bad," Levey said.
Netanyahu came to power 11 months ago vowing to deregulate the economy, reform the capital markets and privatise nearly 100 companies.
But faced with a sputtering Middle East peace process, Netanyahu has had little time to devote to the economy.
A new government at this point would be welcomed by many investors.
"I don't think it will be a big loss to the market if he (Netanyahu) goes," Levey said. "The new prime minister will probably be better as far as the market is concerned."
Whatever the political outcome, it is likely to have only a short-term effect on the stock market, analysts say.
"In the long term, the market is heavily driven by interest rates. And real rates have come down significantly," Levey said.
